meta.title: Social Engineering Incident Atlas India
meta.research_data_version: v0.2.2 corrective expansion / v0.2.0 actor schema
meta.sampling_notice: The Atlas is purposively sampled and retrieval-driven. Case counts describe the reviewed corpus and must not be interpreted as national cybercrime prevalence or state rankings.
meta.attribution_notice: Actor records assess source-supported conduct and identity resolution. They are not findings of guilt.
meta.map_notice: Map markers show the state or UT coded for reviewed incidents. Marker location is an approximate state centroid, not an incident coordinate.
meta.citation: Hamzah. (2026). Social Engineering Incident Atlas India (v0.2.2). GitHub repository.

cases.case_title: Ramakrishna Mission Gwalior digital arrest fraud
cases.court_or_authority: High Court of Madhya Pradesh, Gwalior Bench
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Inspector / police official from Nashik Police
cases.reconnaissance_description: The caller used the complainant's name and claimed that a Canara Bank account had been opened using his Aadhaar details, but the public court record does not establish how those details were obtained.
cases.initial_contact_summary: On 17 March 2025 the Secretary of Ramakrishna Mission Ashram, Thatipur, Gwalior received a WhatsApp call from a person claiming to be an Inspector from Nashik Police.
cases.pretext_summary: The caller claimed that an FIR for money laundering had been registered, presented details of a purported Canara Bank account in the complainant's name with about INR 20 crore in transactions, sent a PDF bank statement via WhatsApp, and said the complainant had to cooperate with an investigation to avoid arrest.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Legitimacy theatre using police uniform, a police-office visual setting, purported official financial documents, secrecy instructions, and coercive compliance.
cases.requested_action: Cooperate with the purported investigation, disclose personal/family and Ashram financial information, remain available and isolated from outside verification, and transfer Ashram funds to accounts specified by the caller.
cases.victim_action: The complainant continued communicating, disclosed information, followed secrecy/isolation instructions, and transferred a total of INR 25,299,000 to multiple accounts between 17 March and 11 April 2025.
cases.other_evidence: Purported bank-statement PDF; memorandum statements; cheque/withdrawal records; mobile phone and SIM seizure; later court order recounts CDR relationships among several accused.
cases.attribution_target: Identified downstream accused network associated with communications and movement of funds; the original impersonating caller(s) remain unresolved in the public material reviewed.
cases.attribution_limitations: The public court material links several accused to beneficiary accounts, withdrawals, bank facilitation, devices, or communications with other accused, but does not conclusively identify the person who made the original WhatsApp impersonation call or prove that every downstream account holder knew the full social-engineering scheme.
cases.alternative_explanation: For some accused, the documented link may be limited to account provision, withdrawal, transaction facilitation, device/SIM association, or communication with co-accused rather than direct participation in the initial impersonation. Knowledge and intent remain matters for trial.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Direct digital attribution of the original WhatsApp caller(s), ideally through platform/provider records, device-level account artefacts, telecom correlation, and authenticated communication records tying the impersonation account to an operator.
cases.legal_provisions: BNS 61(2); BNS 111(3) (in some orders); BNS 238; BNS 319(2); BNS 318(4); BNS 308(2); BNS 336(2); BNS 337; BNS 338; BNS 336(3); BNS 340(2); Information Technology Act Section 66-D
cases.disposition: Trial remains pending in the public court material reviewed. Multiple accused have pursued bail or quashing applications. The latest direct order located for this coding pass, dated 6 May 2026, dismissed Ravi Kumar Sahani's second bail application.
cases.case_summary: According to repeated Madhya Pradesh High Court recitals of the prosecution case, the Secretary of Ramakrishna Mission Ashram in Gwalior was contacted on WhatsApp on 17 March 2025 by a person claiming to be a Nashik Police Inspector. The caller alleged that a money-laundering FIR concerned a Canara Bank account purportedly opened in the complainant's name, sent a PDF account statement, threatened arrest, and later used a video call showing a police-uniformed person in a police-office-like setting. The complainant was instructed not to disclose the interaction and was induced to provide financial information and transfer Ashram funds. Between 17 March and 11 April 2025, INR 25,299,000 was transferred to multiple accounts. Later court orders describe bank-account trails, withdrawals, seized phones/SIMs, and CDR links among several accused. The reviewed public material supports meaningful attribution to parts of the downstream transaction and communications network, but it does not conclusively identify the original impersonating caller.
cases.research_notes: Primary coding privileges repeated High Court recitals over early press reports where details conflict. An NDTV report states that funds went to 12 accounts and describes a 26-day episode; this supports known_account_count=12. Early press reporting contains some inconsistent details about the first contact and impersonated agency, so those details were not used where they conflicted with the judicial record. Pre-publication source audit completed 2026-08-16; structured coding rechecked against the registered public source(s). v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

actors.conduct_assessed: WhatsApp voice/video police impersonation, threats, secrecy/isolation, information elicitation and transfer instructions.
actors.attribution_limitations: The public material reconstructs the conduct but does not identify the human operator of the impersonating WhatsApp account.
actors.relationship_note: May overlap with downstream actors, but the reviewed record does not establish that overlap.

actors.conduct_assessed: Receiving and moving victim funds through multiple beneficiary/intermediary accounts.
actors.attribution_limitations: Financial and communications linkage does not establish that every account-linked person knew the full scheme or conducted the original impersonation.
actors.alternative_explanation: Some account-linked persons may have had narrower facilitation or mule roles.
actors.relationship_note: Cluster summarises several downstream roles rather than treating all accused as equivalent.

actors.conduct_assessed: Withdrawing, clearing or cashing out portions of transferred fraud proceeds.
actors.attribution_limitations: Cash-out activity does not establish participation in the initial impersonation or full knowledge of the scheme.
actors.alternative_explanation: A person may have handled or withdrawn funds without being the victim-facing operator.
actors.relationship_note: May overlap with the beneficiary-account cluster, but the assessed conduct is different.

actors.conduct_assessed: Allegedly facilitating cheque clearance, withdrawal and transfer activity involving fraud-linked funds while working as a bank cashier.
actors.attribution_limitations: The court treated the facilitation evidence as prima facie at bail stage; it does not establish participation in the original police impersonation, and knowledge/intent remained for trial.
actors.alternative_explanation: The defence argued that the cashier acted on manager-approved vouchers and lacked knowledge of the fraudulent source of funds.
actors.relationship_note: Specific financial-facilitation role, separated from the original caller and other account actors.

actors.conduct_assessed: Allegedly arranging/purchasing bank accounts and account kits for use in moving cyber-fraud proceeds.
actors.attribution_limitations: The order records a co-accused disclosure and case-diary material supporting account procurement, but this remains bail-stage evidence and does not identify the original caller.
actors.alternative_explanation: The defence argued there was no direct evidence that the actor was the caller and challenged the downstream linkage.
actors.relationship_note: Specific account-procurement role separated from other downstream actors.

actors.conduct_assessed: Allegedly providing a third-party bank account on rent for transactions involving fraud proceeds and receiving consideration.
actors.attribution_limitations: The court relied on bank-account details and a memorandum statement at bail stage; the role does not establish victim-facing impersonation or the full conspiracy.
actors.alternative_explanation: The defence argued there was no direct caller evidence and challenged attribution of the broader conspiracy.
actors.relationship_note: Specific account-provision role separated from the original caller and other financial actors.

cases.case_title: VIP Profit Makers fake investment app fraud
cases.court_or_authority: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Person claiming to be Karan Subhash Arora, Assistant to Manager at MUNOTH CAPITAL LTD
cases.initial_contact_summary: In August 2025, the complainant received a WhatsApp call from a person claiming association with MUNOTH CAPITAL LTD and offering investment plans.
cases.pretext_summary: The caller claimed membership in a SEBI-listed investment company, added the complainant to a WhatsApp group named VIP PROFIT MAKERS with about 100 members, showed apparent examples of money doubling, and induced him to install an ALFA NAVIGATOR app and transfer funds to accounts supplied through the app.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Social proof through a large WhatsApp group and apparent examples of profitable investments; legitimacy borrowing from a claimed SEBI-listed company and an app-store link.
cases.requested_action: Join the investment group, install/register on ALFA NAVIGATOR, and transfer investment funds to designated bank accounts.
cases.victim_action: The complainant transferred multiple amounts to several bank accounts and later attempted to withdraw his funds.
cases.other_evidence: FIR reproduces the WhatsApp contact, app URL, named group, and detailed beneficiary bank accounts and transfer amounts.
cases.attribution_target: Petitioner Shivam Goyal and any operators of the WhatsApp group / app infrastructure.
cases.attribution_limitations: The bail order reproduces a detailed victim narrative but gives little detail explaining how the petitioner was technically or financially linked to the original inducement, beyond the fact that he was arrested and prosecuted in the FIR.
cases.alternative_explanation: The petitioner claimed that he had himself been duped by another person and was falsely implicated.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Specific digital or financial evidence connecting the petitioner to operation of the WhatsApp identity, ALFA NAVIGATOR infrastructure, or beneficiary accounts.
cases.disposition: Regular bail granted on 27 February 2026; trial pending and merits left open.
cases.case_summary: A Gurugram complainant was approached on WhatsApp by a purported representative of an investment company, added to a large group displaying apparent investment success, and induced to install a fake investment app. He transferred INR 8,248,021 to multiple bank accounts. When withdrawal was attempted, further money was demanded. The public bail order provides a rich social-engineering reconstruction but limited accused-specific attribution evidence.
cases.research_notes: Useful example of social proof and legitimacy engineering in fake-investment fraud. Known account count is seven distinct beneficiary accounts; the source lists nine transfers, with two account numbers reused. Pre-publication source audit completed 2026-08-16; structured coding rechecked against the registered public source(s). v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

actors.attribution_limitations: The source reconstructs the interaction but does not identify the human operator of the WhatsApp persona/group.
actors.relationship_note: May overlap with the app operator or financial actors, but this is not established.

actors.function_assignment_basis: no paper-specific evidence assigning either primary function
actors.conduct_assessed: Operating or controlling the app/infrastructure through which investment activity and payment instructions were presented.
actors.attribution_limitations: No operator-side hosting, account-control, device or provider evidence is described.
actors.relationship_note: Could overlap with the WhatsApp group operator, but the source does not establish this.

actors.conduct_assessed: Receiving the complainant transfers across seven distinct beneficiary accounts.
actors.attribution_limitations: The source identifies accounts and transfers but gives little evidence of who controlled each account or knew the wider fraud.
actors.alternative_explanation: Some accounts may have functioned as mule/intermediary accounts.
actors.relationship_note: Financial layer only.

actors.actor_label: Bail applicant with unspecified alleged scheme role
actors.function_assignment_basis: no paper-specific evidence assigning either primary function
actors.conduct_assessed: Alleged participation in the fraud for which the applicant was arrested and prosecuted.
actors.attribution_limitations: The source does not provide a sufficiently specific evidentiary chain to assign a stable operational role.
actors.alternative_explanation: The applicant claimed that he had himself been duped and falsely implicated.

cases.case_title: Fake HR work-from-home task scam
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Woman calling herself Akansha, purported HR executive of Freelance Pvt. Ltd.
cases.initial_contact_summary: The complainant received a WhatsApp call from a woman presenting herself as an HR executive and offering paid work-from-home Google search/review tasks.
cases.pretext_summary: The caller promised payment for simple tasks, made small initial payments to build trust, then claimed free task coupons had expired and induced the complainant to pay for higher-income tasks.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Trust seeding through genuine small payouts before escalating to paid tasks; sunk-cost pressure when further payments were demanded to recover supposed earnings.
cases.requested_action: Perform online tasks, then make repeated payments for higher-return tasks and additional payments to unlock earnings.
cases.victim_action: The complainant made repeated deposits and lost INR 375,000.
cases.other_evidence: Calling numbers traced to waho.pro, hosted on a U.S.-based server; bank CCTV recorded cash withdrawal; WhatsApp chats recovered from a co-accused phone showed account details being shared.
cases.attribution_target: Aayush Goyal's alleged role in supplying/circulating mule bank accounts, distinct from the original HR impersonator.
cases.attribution_limitations: The complainant did not directly identify the applicant as the inducer. His alleged role arose through co-accused disclosures and WhatsApp chats showing bank-account sharing, rather than direct evidence that he made the original call.
cases.alternative_explanation: The applicant argued that his cryptocurrency-related activity was legitimate and that he neither received cheated money nor knew the complainant.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Direct linkage between the original HR impersonation account/calling infrastructure and identified human operators, plus full cryptocurrency transaction records tying mule-account circulation to fraudulent proceeds.
cases.disposition: Anticipatory bail granted on 15 December 2025; investigation and trial-related proceedings remained ongoing.
cases.case_summary: A Delhi complainant was approached through WhatsApp by a fake HR executive offering paid Google review tasks. Small initial payouts established trust, after which the victim was induced to pay for higher-value tasks and to make additional deposits when attempting to recover earnings, losing INR 375,000. Investigation traced funds through mule accounts, CCTV-recorded withdrawals and WhatsApp account-sharing chats, illustrating a multi-layered separation between social-engineering operators and financial infrastructure.
cases.research_notes: The source reports the calling infrastructure as waho.pro on a U.S.-based server, supporting a cross-border infrastructure dimension even though the victim and investigated network were in India. Pre-publication source audit completed 2026-08-16; structured coding rechecked against the registered public source(s). v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

actors.conduct_assessed: Impersonating an HR executive, offering paid review tasks, seeding trust with small payouts and escalating to paid tasks.
actors.attribution_limitations: The applicant in the proceeding was not directly identified as this caller.
actors.relationship_note: Separated from account-supply and cash-out roles.

actors.conduct_assessed: Allegedly supplying/circulating mule bank-account details used by the fraud network.
actors.attribution_limitations: The evidence supports an alleged financial-infrastructure role, not that this actor made the original HR call.
actors.alternative_explanation: The applicant argued that his cryptocurrency activity was legitimate and that he did not know the complainant.
actors.relationship_note: This is the role assessed in the existing incident-level attribution field.

actors.conduct_assessed: Withdrawing fraud-linked funds from a beneficiary account and handing cash onward in the downstream chain.
actors.attribution_limitations: Bank CCTV and the money trail support the withdrawal role, but this does not establish authorship of the original HR impersonation or control of the wider scheme.
actors.alternative_explanation: Cash-out can establish a downstream role without authorship of fraud communications.
actors.relationship_note: Identified downstream cash-out role, distinct from the account-supply actor and fake HR caller.

actors.function_assignment_basis: no paper-specific evidence assigning either primary function
actors.conduct_assessed: Operating or controlling the calling infrastructure associated with the victim contact.
actors.attribution_limitations: The investigation traced calling numbers to waho.pro and noted U.S. hosting, but operator-side inquiry was still pending and no human operator was identified.
actors.relationship_note: Technical layer separated from the financial layer.

cases.case_title: Canada relative and medical emergency impersonation fraud
cases.court_or_authority: High Court of Punjab and Haryana
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Relative Satpal said to be living in Canada; second caller posed as bank official; third caller posed as Harjeet Singh.
cases.reconnaissance_description: The impersonator used the name of a real Canada-based relative and the victim's bank-account details in the pretext, but the public source does not establish whether this resulted from prior reconnaissance, leaked data, or another route.
cases.initial_contact_summary: The complainant received a WhatsApp call from a person claiming to be his Canada-based relative Satpal.
cases.pretext_summary: The impersonator claimed he would send INR 16.15 lakh to the complainant before returning to India, sent a fake transfer receipt, and a separate caller posed as an Axis Bank head-office employee to corroborate the transfer. The fake relative then requested urgent funds for a purported associate's hospitalized wife.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Layered corroboration using an apparent bank official; emotional pressure through a crying caller and medical emergency; exploitation of kinship and reciprocity after a fake incoming transfer.
cases.requested_action: Provide bank details/blank cheque image and urgently transfer INR 400,000, followed by a request for an additional INR 200,000.
cases.victim_action: The complainant sent a blank cheque image and transferred INR 400,000 before challenging the impersonator with family-verification questions.
cases.other_evidence: Fake INR 16.15 lakh transfer receipt sent on WhatsApp; beneficiary account belonged to petitioner's mother and had petitioner's mobile number registered.
cases.attribution_target: Petitioner Ratan Lal's alleged downstream role connected to the beneficiary account and registered mobile number.
cases.attribution_limitations: The order does not establish that the petitioner made the relative, bank-official, or medical-emergency calls. The bank account was in his mother's name and the petitioner disputed inducement.
cases.alternative_explanation: The petitioner may have been associated with the beneficiary account without being the social-engineering caller; knowledge and commission allegations remained prosecution claims.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Direct linkage of the impersonating WhatsApp/phone numbers to the human operators and authenticated device/platform records showing coordination with the beneficiary account.
cases.legal_provisions: BNS 318(4); BNS 319; BNS 336(3); BNS 338; BNS 340; BNS 61(B) as reported in source
cases.disposition: Regular bail granted on 21 January 2026; trial ongoing.
cases.case_summary: A Haryana victim was contacted on WhatsApp by a person impersonating a real relative living in Canada. The scheme used a forged transfer receipt and a second caller posing as an Axis Bank official to make the fake INR 16.15 lakh incoming transfer appear genuine. The relative then invoked a medical emergency and a crying third caller to induce an urgent INR 400,000 transfer. The victim detected the fraud by asking personal family questions the impersonator could not answer.
cases.research_notes: This case is especially valuable for studying layered corroboration, emotional urgency, and family-knowledge verification as a defensive social-engineering countermeasure. Pre-publication source audit completed 2026-08-16; structured coding rechecked against the registered public source(s). v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

actors.conduct_assessed: Impersonating the victim real Canada-based relative, presenting the fake incoming transfer and requesting emergency funds.
actors.attribution_limitations: The human operator is not identified in the reviewed order.
actors.relationship_note: May overlap with other callers, but the source presents distinct personas.

actors.conduct_assessed: Impersonating an Axis Bank head-office employee to corroborate the fictitious incoming transfer.
actors.attribution_limitations: No telecom, device or platform record identifies the caller.
actors.relationship_note: Could be the same human as another caller; identity equivalence is not inferred.

actors.conduct_assessed: Using emotional distress and a medical-emergency narrative to reinforce the urgent payment request.
actors.attribution_limitations: The operator identity and relationship to the other personas are not established.
actors.relationship_note: Persona may have been operated by the same person as another role, but no inference is made.

actors.conduct_assessed: Alleged downstream connection to the account that received the victim INR 400,000 transfer.
actors.attribution_limitations: The order does not establish that this actor made any of the relative, bank-official or medical-emergency calls; account control/knowledge is contested.
actors.alternative_explanation: The actor may have been associated with the beneficiary account without being a social-engineering operator.
actors.relationship_note: Financial role deliberately separated from all three victim-facing personas.

cases.case_title: Fake Yahoo customer care APK fraud against senior citizen
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Purported customer-care service for Yahoo email issue
cases.initial_contact_summary: A senior citizen searching online for help with a Yahoo email problem contacted a purported customer-care number found through an online search.
cases.pretext_summary: The purported support operator induced the complainant to download an APK and persuaded him to provide debit-card details while ostensibly resolving the email problem.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Search-result trust transfer: the victim treated a number surfaced through online search as legitimate customer support.
cases.requested_action: Download an APK and provide debit-card information.
cases.victim_action: The complainant downloaded the APK and disclosed debit-card details; about INR 14 lakh was initially siphoned and linked fixed deposits were later accessed/liquidated, raising the reported total loss to about INR 26 lakh.
cases.other_evidence: KYC/account-opening documents, transaction statements, CDRs, IPDRs, IMEI data, location charts, ATM CCTV and NCRP-linked account information.
cases.attribution_target: Sahil Khan's alleged cash-out / beneficiary role within an inter-State fraud network, separate from the fake customer-care operator.
cases.attribution_limitations: The public order strongly links the applicant to cash withdrawals, location data and receipt of funds but does not establish that he operated the fake customer-care number or APK.
cases.alternative_explanation: The applicant denied any role and argued that location coincidence was insufficient; original social-engineering and malware operators remain distinct from downstream cash-out actors.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Direct forensic attribution of the fake customer-care number/APK infrastructure and proof linking that operator layer to the downstream financial network.
cases.disposition: Anticipatory bail denied on 14 January 2026; investigation continuing.
cases.case_summary: A Delhi senior citizen searching online for Yahoo support contacted a fraudulent customer-care number, downloaded an APK and disclosed card information. The reported loss eventually reached about INR 26 lakh after linked fixed deposits were accessed. Investigation used bank KYC and transactions, CDR/IPDR/IMEI/location data and ATM CCTV to map an inter-State mule and cash-out network. The case illustrates the evidentiary separation between the social-engineering entry point and downstream financial actors.
cases.research_notes: One of the strongest cases in the pilot for combining human manipulation, malicious software installation and layered digital/physical attribution evidence. Pre-publication source audit completed 2026-08-16; structured coding rechecked against the registered public source(s). v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

actors.attribution_limitations: The public order does not identify the human operator of the fake support number.
actors.relationship_note: Victim-facing role separated from later cash-out network.

actors.relationship_note: Could overlap with the support caller, but this is not established.

cases.case_title: Tekku Samurai cross-border tech-support fraud
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Microsoft or Apple representatives
cases.reconnaissance_description: Call-centre devices contained lists of Japanese telephone numbers and scripts/quotations, indicating systematic targeting of Japanese victims.
cases.initial_contact_summary: Victims encountered fake virus alerts/phishing prompts on malicious URLs and were instructed to call a displayed number.
cases.pretext_summary: Callers impersonating Microsoft or Apple claimed the victim's computer had technical problems, induced installation of remote-access software or purchase of antivirus/service packages, and obtained access to sensitive financial information.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Panic induction through fake virus alerts and brand impersonation, followed by scripted technical authority and remote-assistance framing.
cases.requested_action: Call the displayed number, install remote-access software or purchase purported technical services, and provide/payment-sensitive information.
cases.victim_action: Victims installed remote-access software and/or paid through gift cards or other channels; four Japanese victims were specifically identified in the FIR.
cases.remote_access_tool: Remote-access software; seized systems also showed Zoiper VoIP use
cases.other_evidence: SSDs, call logs, Japanese phone-number lists, fake Microsoft identity cards, victim banking screenshots, gift-card screenshots/codes, pitching scripts and quotations, partnership/rent/KYC records and bank profit transfers.
cases.attribution_target: Tekku Samurai call-centre operation and Komal Kumar's alleged ownership/management role.
cases.attribution_limitations: The order concerns bail and does not finally adjudicate guilt. It does not establish that the applicant personally made each victim call; the strength code concerns ownership/operational linkage to the documented call-centre system.
cases.alternative_explanation: The applicant argued he was merely an owner and that financial transfers from Bidder Media were legitimate commercial transactions unrelated to victim fraud.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Victim-specific linkage between particular call-centre agents/sessions and each fraudulent loss, plus complete foreign payment and remote-access logs.
cases.legal_provisions: BNS 61(2); BNS 308; BNS 318(4); BNS 319(2); IT Act 66C; IT Act 66D; IT Act 66 read with 43
cases.disposition: Regular bail denied on 2 February 2026; supplementary charge sheet had been filed.
cases.case_summary: CBI alleged that an India-based call centre in Varanasi targeted Japanese computer users through malicious virus pop-ups and phishing prompts, then impersonated Microsoft or Apple personnel to induce remote access and payment. Searches recovered devices containing fake IDs, victim banking images, gift-card data, Japanese call lists, scripts and VoIP logs. Partnership, KYC, rent and bank records linked the applicant to the call-centre business. This is the pilot's clearest example of social engineering embedded in an organised technical infrastructure.
cases.research_notes: Cross-border case included because the investigated operation and evidence were materially situated in India even though the named victims were in Japan. cases.initial_contact_summary: The victim received an SMS containing a link followed by a phone call from an unknown person.

cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Service-interruption threat used to induce a security-sensitive action.

cases.legal_provisions: RBI Circular dated 06.07.2017 on customer liability for unauthorised electronic banking transactions
cases.disposition: Delhi High Court Division Bench allowed SBI's appeal on 29 May 2026 and set aside the earlier single-judge judgment; it stressed that unresolved technical questions required forensic examination rather than inference in writ proceedings.
cases.case_summary: An academician received an SMS link and a call warning that his SMS service would be closed unless he clicked. After doing so, two internet-banking transactions totalling INR 260,000 were executed. The victim denied sharing OTPs. The later appellate judgment is especially valuable for the Atlas because the court refused to infer the exact compromise mechanism without technical or forensic evidence, highlighting the gap between a documented social-engineering trigger and unresolved technical causation.
cases.research_notes: This is a civil/banking-liability case rather than a criminal prosecution, included because the underlying social-engineering incident and evidentiary uncertainty are richly documented. cases.case_summary: An employee received payment requests through the WhatsApp account of his reporting officer, a senior public-sector executive, and transferred INR 45,000 before a third request prompted verification. cases.reconnaissance_description: The messages referred to the complainant’s pending property litigation and promised influence over a favourable court order, showing case-specific knowledge even though its source was not established.
cases.initial_contact_summary: The complainant received repeated messages/calls and a letter from a person presenting himself as a court-connected operator who could influence a pending property case.
cases.pretext_summary: The sender demanded INR 15–20 lakh in exchange for securing a favourable court outcome and threatened death if the demand was not met. The prosecution later attempted to connect the communications to accused persons through SIM/CAF/CDR and related electronic material.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Claimed privileged access to judicial/police systems coupled with violent threats.

cases.victim_action: The public judgment describes repeated demands and threats but does not establish delivery of the demanded property; the court treated the extortion case as unproved.
cases.other_evidence: The prosecution relied on CAF/KYC, CDR and other secondary electronic records, but the court identified conflicting SIM-registration evidence, missing witnesses and invalid Section 65-B certification.
cases.attribution_target: Accused persons alleged to have operated the court-connected persona and threatening communications.

cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Admissible, authenticated telecom/electronic records and reliable subscriber/device evidence connecting the critical communications to the accused human operators.
cases.legal_provisions: IPC 419; IPC 420; IPC 386; IPC 506; IPC 201; IPC 511; IPC 34; IT Act 66A (as charged/recorded)

cases.pretext_summary: The callers escalated the courier story into a criminal-prosecution threat, presented themselves as Mumbai Cyber Crime police and said the complainant had to pay money to save herself from prosecution.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Courier-to-police escalation, narcotics accusation and fear of criminal prosecution.
cases.requested_action: Transfer funds purportedly required to avoid or resolve the threatened criminal prosecution.
cases.victim_action: The complainant transferred INR 4,499,996. The investigation traced major portions through specific bank accounts and onward transfers/withdrawals.
cases.other_evidence: The court relied on account statements, National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal cash-flow information and investigation findings concerning account opening, onward transfers and cash withdrawal.
cases.attribution_target: Applicant’s alleged account-control/routing role and other accused persons’ cash-out/financial roles, distinct from the original FedEx/police callers.
cases.attribution_limitations: The bail order provides strong prima facie financial linkage to the applicant’s account but does not establish that the applicant made the original FedEx or police impersonation calls; the investigation was still preliminary.
cases.alternative_explanation: A bank-account routing role can be narrower than operation of the victim-facing digital-arrest pretext.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Telecom/device evidence identifying the original FedEx and police impersonators and linking those callers to the financial-routing network.
cases.legal_provisions: IPC 419; IPC 420; IT Act 66C; IT Act 66D
cases.disposition: Pre-arrest bail dismissed on 19 March 2026; the Kerala High Court held the investigation was at a preliminary stage and custodial interrogation was necessary.
cases.case_summary: A Kerala complainant was told that a FedEx parcel to Taiwan contained narcotics and was then threatened by callers posing as Mumbai Cyber Crime police. She transferred about INR 4.5 million. The bail record distinguishes the unidentified victim-facing callers from account controllers and cash-out actors traced through the financial investigation.
cases.research_notes: Cross-border dimension reflects the Taiwan courier pretext and multi-state financial routing, not proof that the human operators were outside India. cases.case_title: Spoofed CBI and MHA official impersonation extortion conspiracy
cases.case_number: Criminal Revision Case No.199/2025; C.C.No.6061/2024; CBI RC 01(A)/2020
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Senior Government of India officials associated with CBI/MHA and related official influence
cases.reconnaissance_description: The alleged scheme targeted persons facing investigations and used case-specific promises of favourable intervention, official identities/numbers and intermediary relationships.
cases.initial_contact_summary: The prosecution alleged a conspiracy in which spoofed official government numbers and intermediaries were used to approach persons facing investigations.
cases.pretext_summary: The actors allegedly impersonated or invoked senior Government of India/CBI/MHA authority, promised favourable settlement of investigative matters and demanded enormous payments, including a source-described INR 100 crore demand in one instance.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Official-number spoofing, claimed access to senior government authority and exploitation of targets’ fear of ongoing investigations.
cases.requested_action: Pay large sums in return for purported influence over or favourable resolution of investigative/criminal matters.
cases.victim_action: The reviewed revision order describes demands and attempted extortion; it does not establish a completed focal transfer suitable for coding as financial loss.
cases.other_evidence: The prosecution material described WhatsApp chats, telephonic surveillance, spoofed calls from official government numbers, witness statements and alleged coordination among accused persons.
cases.attribution_target: Petitioner’s alleged coordinator/conspiracy role in an extortion-by-impersonation network.
cases.attribution_limitations: The High Court was reviewing a discharge/revision question, not deciding guilt. It found sufficient material to proceed but expressly left proof of the charges to trial.
cases.alternative_explanation: The petitioner argued that he was himself a victim/was excluded from the core conspiracy and that the prosecution material did not conclusively establish his involvement.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Trial-tested evidence connecting each spoofed call, government persona and extortion demand to specific human operators and establishing the petitioner’s knowledge/intent beyond the charge-stage threshold.
cases.legal_provisions: IPC 120B; IPC 419; IPC 420; IPC 384 and related conspiracy/extortion provisions as recorded in underlying proceedings
cases.disposition: Telangana High Court dismissed the criminal revision on 2 March 2026, holding there was sufficient material for the petitioner to face trial and that a mini-trial was impermissible at the discharge stage.
cases.case_summary: A CBI-investigated conspiracy allegedly used spoofed official government numbers and claimed access to senior CBI/MHA officials to demand huge payments from persons facing investigations in return for favourable outcomes. The case expands the Atlas into official-influence extortion and is useful for separating charge-stage evidentiary sufficiency from final attribution.
cases.research_notes: No financial_loss_inr is coded because the reviewed order describes demands, including INR 100 crore, but does not establish a completed focal payment. Second-pass source-to-code and privacy audit completed 2026-08-26. v0.2.0 full-corpus source-to-code re-audit completed 2026-09-04.

cases.case_title: Tony Enterprises SIM-swap and online-banking takeover fraud
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Registered mobile subscriber identity used to obtain a duplicate SIM
cases.initial_contact_summary: An unknown person approached the telecom service provider and fraudulently represented himself as the registered subscriber in order to obtain a duplicate SIM.
cases.pretext_summary: The impostor sought a duplicate SIM in the subscriber's identity; once the legitimate SIM became dysfunctional, OTPs and banking alerts could be received on the fraudulently issued SIM.
cases.requested_action: Obtain control of the registered mobile number and use it to authenticate online-banking transactions.
cases.victim_action: The account holders did not authorize the transfer; after the mobile stopped functioning they discovered unauthorized online transfers.
cases.other_evidence: CBCID investigation reports; duplicate-SIM issuance records; bank transfer trail; IP-address findings.
cases.attribution_target: Unknown SIM-swap operator(s) and downstream beneficiary network
cases.attribution_limitations: The High Court records investigative findings on the mechanism and financial trail, but the public judgment does not fully resolve the identity and specific conduct of every human operator.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Subscriber-acquisition records, CCTV/device evidence and authenticated bank-login artefacts tying the duplicate-SIM request and account access to specific operators.
cases.disposition: Writ petitions disposed with directions concerning disputed fraudulent banking transactions; criminal investigation findings were discussed but individual criminal guilt was not adjudicated.
cases.case_summary: Tony Enterprises and Tony Lites lost INR 1,625,000 after a duplicate SIM was issued to a person impersonating the registered subscriber. The Kerala High Court recorded CBCID findings that the fraudsters used duplicate SIMs, OTPs and unauthorized online-bank access, with funds transferred to accounts in West Bengal and Maharashtra.

cases.impersonated_identity_detail: HDFC Bank NET Banking software-upgrade communication
cases.initial_contact_summary: The complainant received an email on 23 August 2008 purporting to come from HDFC Bank NET Banking and directing him to a software-upgrade link.
cases.pretext_summary: The message represented that HDFC Bank was conducting a software upgrade and induced the complainant to use a linked page that captured his customer ID and I-Pin password.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Institutional legitimacy was borrowed from HDFC branding and normal net-banking maintenance language.
cases.requested_action: Visit the linked HDFC-looking page and enter net-banking credentials.
cases.victim_action: The complainant followed the link and entered his customer ID and I-Pin; unauthorized beneficiaries were later added and INR 223,960 was transferred.
cases.other_evidence: CERT-In phishing-infrastructure analysis; Section 65-B certificates; account-opening forms; ATM/debit card and cheque evidence; three mobile phones and two SIM cards sent to GEQD Hyderabad.
cases.attribution_target: Freeman Anosike Aluma's alleged coordination/receipt role and the unresolved phishing operator(s).
cases.attribution_limitations: The trial conviction was set aside because a potentially vital GEQD expert report on three phones and two SIM cards had not been placed before the trial court. The public appellate record does not establish that the appellant personally sent the phishing email or operated the phishing website.
cases.alternative_explanation: The appellant denied involvement and argued that actual beneficiaries had been treated as witnesses; the missing expert report could materially affect the technical linkage.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: The GEQD expert report and device-level evidence capable of connecting a specific human to the phishing infrastructure and relevant communications.
cases.legal_provisions: IPC Section 379; IPC Section 120-B; Information Technology Act Section 66
cases.disposition: Trial conviction and sentence were set aside on 16 October 2018 and the matter was remanded for fresh appreciation after obtaining/considering the GEQD expert report.
cases.case_summary: A bank customer received a fake HDFC software-upgrade email, followed a link and disclosed net-banking credentials. Three beneficiaries were added and INR 223,960 was transferred. The investigation produced bank records, subscriber forms, CDRs, login/IP evidence, Section 65-B certificates and CERT-In analysis showing infrastructure routed through multiple countries. Witness evidence linked the appellant to arrangement and receipt of cash from a beneficiary account. However, three mobile phones and two SIM cards had been sent for GEQD examination and the resulting expert report was never placed before the trial court. The appellate court treated that omission as sufficiently important to set aside the conviction and remand the case. The record therefore combines a rich phishing reconstruction with a major evidentiary gap at the human-attribution layer.
cases.research_notes: Wave 1A corrective expansion. Exact incident dates are supported by the appellate record. Cross-border coding reflects documented US/France/Germany/Canada infrastructure, not a finding about offender nationality. Conviction status is not_yet_adjudicated because the trial conviction was set aside and the case remanded.

cases.case_title: Fake Louis Philippe refund support and malicious-app fraud
cases.case_number: WA/364/2022; WP(C) No.1900/2022; Jalukbari P.S. Case No.1229/2021
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Louis Philippe customer-care manager handling a garment refund
cases.reconnaissance_description: The victim had recently purchased a Louis Philippe garment online and later received a brand-specific refund call. The brand subsequently reported a customer-database breach during the relevant period.
cases.initial_contact_summary: The victim received a phone call from a person posing as Louis Philippe customer care after seeking to return an online garment purchase.
cases.pretext_summary: The caller offered to process a INR 4,000 refund and instructed the victim to download a mobile application.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Brand-specific knowledge and refund context created legitimacy; later records noted a customer-data breach at the retailer.
cases.requested_action: Download a mobile application to receive a refund.
cases.victim_action: The victim downloaded the application; three unauthorized transactions totalling INR 94,204 followed.
cases.other_evidence: Bank transaction records, beneficiary-account records, OTP logs, complaint records and retailer email acknowledging a customer-database breach.
cases.attribution_target: Papendra Kumar's caller/beneficiary role and downstream transfer recipients.
cases.attribution_limitations: The appellate consumer/writ record identifies Papendra Kumar as the fraudster/respondent and documents a beneficiary account in his name, but it is not a criminal conviction and does not independently establish every technical step performed through the downloaded application.
cases.alternative_explanation: The proceeding centered on bank/customer liability, not a criminal trial of the identified respondent.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Device/application forensic evidence showing what the downloaded app did and directly tying the caller's device/account activity to the unauthorized transactions.
cases.legal_provisions: IPC Section 417; IPC Section 420
cases.disposition: Gauhati High Court dismissed SBI's writ appeal and upheld the direction to credit the unauthorized-transaction amount to the customer.
cases.case_summary: A Guwahati customer who wanted to return a Louis Philippe garment received a refund call from a person posing as the brand's customer-care manager. The caller instructed him to download a mobile app to receive INR 4,000. Three unauthorized transactions totalling INR 94,204 followed. The record identified Papendra Kumar as the caller/respondent, traced a substantial transfer to an account in his name and documented later movement of funds. The retailer also acknowledged a customer-database breach during the relevant period. The High Court treated the transactions as unauthorized and upheld relief against SBI. The case combines pretext-specific targeting, device compromise and a comparatively unusual overlap between a human-resolved victim-facing actor and a financial endpoint.
cases.research_notes: Identity resolution does not imply criminal guilt. The High Court proceeding adjudicated banking liability rather than criminal responsibility.

actors.function_assignment_basis: The appellate record identifies him as the fraudster/customer-care caller and describes a beneficiary account in his name receiving a substantial transfer.
actors.conduct_assessed: Posing as Louis Philippe customer care, inducing app download and controlling/receiving a beneficiary endpoint.
actors.attribution_limitations: The proceeding adjudicated bank/customer liability rather than criminal guilt and does not independently prove every technical action through the app.
actors.alternative_explanation: Criminal responsibility was not the issue finally determined in the writ appeal.
actors.relationship_note: Unusual case where a source resolves both victim-facing and financial functions to the same named human.

actors.function_assignment_basis: The record states funds were moved from the first beneficiary account into other accounts.
actors.conduct_assessed: Receiving onward transfers after the initial unauthorized transaction.
actors.attribution_limitations: The appellate record does not resolve the identities or knowledge of all downstream recipients.

cases.case_title: SBI debit-card verification vishing against senior citizens
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: SBI Debit Card Section employee
cases.reconnaissance_description: The caller knew the newly allotted secret PIN and referred specifically to the recently issued ATM/debit card, indicating access to non-public account/card information, though the source does not establish how it was obtained.
cases.initial_contact_summary: A caller contacted one of the senior-citizen joint account holders and introduced himself as an SBI Debit Card Section employee.
cases.pretext_summary: The caller said the recently issued debit card was blocked pending verification, stated the secret PIN and asked for card particulars.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Possession of the new-card PIN and card-specific knowledge created strong legitimacy.
cases.requested_action: Provide debit-card particulars to complete verification/unblocking.
cases.victim_action: The card particulars were disclosed. The other account holder changed the PIN within minutes, but six withdrawals still reduced the balance from INR 35,527.71 to INR 69.71.
cases.other_evidence: ATM/debit-card transaction history and banking records showing withdrawals despite a changed PIN.
cases.attribution_target: Unresolved caller and the unknown person(s) who executed the withdrawals.
cases.attribution_limitations: The fraudulent caller was not traced and the consumer record does not identify the human operator who made the withdrawals or explain how the caller obtained the newly issued PIN.
cases.alternative_explanation: The dispute focused on bank liability and security-system gaps; it did not resolve criminal authorship.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Telecom/subscriber records and ATM/location/device evidence capable of linking the call and withdrawals to a specific person.
cases.legal_provisions: Consumer Protection Act, 1986
cases.disposition: NCDRC dismissed SBI's revision petition and left the State Commission's direction to re-credit INR 35,458 with interest and compensation intact.
cases.case_summary: Senior-citizen pension account holders had recently received a replacement SBI debit card and PIN. A caller posing as SBI's Debit Card Section knew the secret PIN and said the new card was blocked pending verification. One account holder disclosed card details. Within minutes the other changed the PIN, but six withdrawals nonetheless reduced the account balance from INR 35,527.71 to INR 69.71. The caller was never traced. Consumer adjudication focused on the unexplained ability to withdraw funds even after the PIN change and on bank-system responsibility. The case is valuable because it documents a classic vishing interaction while preserving a major unresolved technical question about how the caller possessed fresh card/PIN information and how the withdrawals were executed.
cases.research_notes: Financial loss uses the INR 35,458 re-credit amount fixed by the State Commission/NCDRC. The record is adjudicatory on consumer liability, not criminal attribution.

actors.actor_label: SBI Debit Card Section impersonating caller
actors.function_assignment_basis: The consumer record reconstructs the call and card-verification pretext but says the caller could not be traced.
actors.conduct_assessed: Calling the senior citizen, stating the fresh PIN and eliciting card particulars under a verification pretext.
actors.attribution_limitations: No subscriber/device evidence in the reviewed source resolves the caller; possession of the new PIN remains unexplained.

actors.function_assignment_basis: Bank records establish six unauthorized withdrawals but not the person who executed them.
actors.conduct_assessed: Executing or benefiting from the six withdrawals after the victim changed the PIN.
actors.attribution_limitations: Transaction evidence establishes loss but not human identity or whether the caller and withdrawal operator were the same person.

cases.case_title: Christina George Facebook, customs and embassy advance-fee fraud
cases.court_or_authority: High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh at Jammu
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Christina George, purported UK visitor/investor; Delhi Airport customs officer; Mr Philip/embassy-linked intermediary
cases.initial_contact_summary: The complainant received a Facebook message in February 2019 from a person using the name Christina George and was moved to WhatsApp and phone communication.
cases.pretext_summary: The persona claimed to be a UK visitor bringing money for investment in India. A second caller posed as a Delhi Airport customs officer, and later another person calling himself Mr Philip demanded further payments to release allegedly seized funds.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Layered personas provided corroboration across a social identity, customs authority and an asserted embassy-related intermediary.
cases.requested_action: Transfer repeated amounts to pay customs/release charges and other purported expenses so the visitor and her seized money could be released.
cases.victim_action: The complainant made repeated transfers to multiple accounts totalling INR 8,858,883.
cases.other_evidence: Account-opening/customer-application records, alleged fake identity documents and investigation of multiple beneficiary accounts.
cases.attribution_target: Rajesh Kumar Kashyap's alleged downstream/organising role and the unresolved multi-persona victim-facing operators.
cases.attribution_limitations: The bail record contains serious allegations based on co-accused disclosure, fake identity documents and linked accounts, but it does not establish that the petitioner personally operated the Christina George/customs/Mr Philip personas. Guilt was not finally adjudicated.
cases.alternative_explanation: The petitioner sought bail and disputed continued custody; the court's order was not a final finding on the prosecution narrative.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Platform, device and telecom evidence directly linking the Facebook/WhatsApp/phone personas to specific human operators and separating them from downstream account/document actors.
cases.legal_provisions: RPC Section 420; RPC Section 465; RPC Section 467; RPC Section 468; RPC Section 471; RPC Section 120-B
cases.disposition: Bail application rejected on 30 July 2021; prosecution allegations and trial remained unresolved on the merits.
cases.case_summary: A Jammu-region complainant was contacted on Facebook by a persona using the name Christina George, who proposed business investment and shifted communication to WhatsApp. A second caller posed as a Delhi Airport customs officer and said Christina's money was being held for customs duty. After the victim transferred funds, the story escalated through further release demands and a third persona, Mr Philip, allegedly connected to embassy assistance. Total transfers reached INR 88,58,883. Investigation traced multiple accounts and alleged use of fabricated identity documents and SIMs. A bail order described Rajesh Kumar Kashyap as an alleged organiser/kingpin based partly on co-accused statements and documentary/account links, but did not establish that he personally operated the victim-facing personas.
cases.research_notes: The source itself contains inconsistent FIR references in different paragraphs; the Atlas stores the bail-application number and avoids harmonising the FIR number. Cross-border=yes reflects the UK/foreign-national dimension alleged in the record, not a finding about the location or nationality of the actual victim-facing operator.

actors.function_assignment_basis: The victim-facing scheme used multiple coordinated personas across Facebook, WhatsApp and phone; real-world humans behind the personas remain unresolved.
actors.conduct_assessed: Operating layered investment, customs and release/embassy personas to induce repeated transfers.
actors.attribution_limitations: The record reconstructs the personas and interaction but does not map each persona to a specific real-world human.
actors.relationship_note: Personas may have been operated by one or several humans.

actors.function_assignment_basis: The bail record alleges a coordinating/kingpin role through co-accused disclosure, false-document/account evidence and investigation of multiple accounts.
actors.conduct_assessed: Alleged organisation of fraudulent identity/account infrastructure and associated financial-fraud activity.
actors.attribution_limitations: Bail-stage allegations do not establish that he operated the focal victim-facing personas; guilt was not finally adjudicated.
actors.alternative_explanation: He sought bail and the proceeding did not determine final criminal responsibility.
actors.relationship_note: Do not collapse alleged organisational role into the Christina/customs/Mr Philip victim-facing layer.

actors.function_assignment_basis: The investigation described multiple accounts and SIMs opened using altered/fabricated identity documents.
actors.conduct_assessed: Providing or controlling bank/SIM endpoints used to receive and route victim funds.
actors.attribution_limitations: The public bail order does not establish equivalent knowledge or conduct for every person connected to the infrastructure.

cases.case_title: PMO Principal Secretary impersonation for government facilities
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister / PMO official and PA
cases.reconnaissance_description: The calls targeted named government offices and officials able to provide contacts, vehicles, accommodation and protocol support.
cases.initial_contact_summary: Government officials in Puducherry received calls from a person claiming to be the Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister or a close relative/special secretary.
cases.pretext_summary: The caller said a daughter or relative/PA had official or personal work in Puducherry and requested contact details, a vehicle, accommodation and protocol assistance.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Hierarchical deference to senior central-government authority was used to obtain assistance from state/UT officials.
cases.requested_action: Provide official contact details, accommodation, transport and related protocol facilities to a purported PMO-linked visitor.
cases.victim_action: Officials exchanged contact information; a government vehicle was allegedly sent and used for local movement, while some officials became suspicious and refused further facilities.
cases.other_evidence: e-KYC/customer application forms, subscriber evidence, Section 161 witness statements and CDRs connecting relevant phone numbers.
cases.attribution_target: Pramod Kumar Singh's alleged PMO impersonation and Vivek Keshavan's alleged PA/beneficiary role.
cases.attribution_limitations: The High Court was reviewing a challenge to framing of charges and assessed only prima facie material. Identity and conspiracy issues remained for trial, and the defence argued that the petitioner's name/number had been misused.
cases.alternative_explanation: Vivek Keshavan argued that accused no.1 used his name and number without criminal participation and that he paid for his own hotel stay.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Trial-tested evidence resolving who spoke on each call and proving or disproving coordinated intent beyond subscriber/CDR association and witness recognition.
cases.legal_provisions: IPC Section 120-B; IPC Section 419; IPC Section 420
cases.disposition: Delhi High Court dismissed Vivek Keshavan's petition challenging the charge-stage orders; charges and merits remained for trial.
cases.case_summary: Government officials in Puducherry received calls from a person representing himself as the Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister, a special secretary or a close PMO-linked authority. The caller sought contact information and protocol support for a purported PA/relative, including a vehicle and accommodation. Some officials became suspicious and refused assistance, while the prosecution alleged that a government vehicle was in fact used by the second accused. The charge-stage record contains e-KYC/customer application forms, subscriber evidence, witness statements, WhatsApp messages and CDRs showing communication among the relevant numbers. The High Court held that the material was sufficient to proceed to trial but did not finally determine guilt. The case expands the Atlas beyond financial fraud into authority-based social engineering designed to obtain government resources and preferential treatment.
cases.research_notes: State coded Puducherry because the principal induced actions and government facilities occurred there, although the reviewing court was Delhi High Court. No financial_loss_inr is coded because the consequence was alleged use of government facilities rather than a quantified monetary loss.

actors.function_assignment_basis: e-KYC/subscriber records, witness statements and CDRs prima facie linked his numbers to repeated PMO impersonation calls.
actors.conduct_assessed: Impersonating the Principal Secretary/PMO-linked authority and seeking official contacts, vehicle, accommodation and protocol assistance.
actors.attribution_limitations: The High Court assessed only charge-stage prima facie material; voice authorship and conspiracy remained for trial.

actors.function_assignment_basis: Witnesses linked him to the PA identity/phone; CDRs showed contact with accused no.1 and the prosecution alleged he used a government vehicle obtained through the deception.
actors.conduct_assessed: Confirming the PA identity during calls and allegedly availing transport obtained through PMO impersonation.
actors.attribution_limitations: The defence claimed his name/number were misused; the High Court left identity/intention issues for trial and did not finally determine guilt.
actors.alternative_explanation: He argued he paid his own hotel costs and that accused no.1 misused his identity.

cases.case_title: Alliance Solution high-return investment and fake-office fraud
cases.case_number: CR. MISC. No.72271 of 2024; Khagaria (Cyber) P.S. Case No.20/2023
cases.platform_primary: Phone / WhatsApp / email / Alliance Solution website
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Alliance Solution share-market investment company and named executives/support staff
cases.initial_contact_summary: The informant received detailed information by phone about a purported share-market company called Alliance Solution.
cases.pretext_summary: The scheme claimed a long operating history, named executives and support staff, promised 25.40% monthly returns, sent forged agreements/KYC material and provided fictitious Bhopal and Bengaluru office addresses.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Corporate-legitimacy theatre, forged contracts/office details and initial monthly payouts reinforced credibility and sunk-cost commitment.
cases.requested_action: Complete KYC/agreement formalities and transfer investment funds to the Alliance Solution bank account.
cases.victim_action: The informant and spouse transferred INR 5,350,000 and initially received INR 583,480 in purported monthly payouts before payments stopped.
cases.other_evidence: Forged agreement papers, purported KYC/IDs, website link, bank account details and investigation of downstream accounts.
cases.attribution_target: Victim-facing Alliance Solution operator cluster and downstream account-linked participants.
cases.attribution_limitations: Names used by the purported company may be personas or asserted organisational identities. The bail order gives only limited actor-specific evidence regarding the petitioner and contains differing figures for deposits identified in her account.
cases.alternative_explanation: The petitioner said funds deposited to her account came from her husband and that she had no knowledge of the cybercrime or share-market scheme.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Authenticated platform/device records linking the named Alliance Solution personas and communications to specific real-world humans, plus complete transaction tracing across recipient accounts.
cases.legal_provisions: IPC Section 419; IPC Section 420; IPC Section 379; IPC Section 467; IPC Section 468; IPC Section 471; IPC Section 120B; IPC Section 34; Information Technology Act Section 66D
cases.disposition: Divya Pandey was granted bail on 5 March 2025; the merits of the prosecution case remained unresolved.
cases.case_summary: A Bihar informant was introduced by phone to a purported share-market company called Alliance Solution. The operators supplied named executives, a URL, WhatsApp communications, email, forged agreement/KYC papers and office addresses in Bhopal and Bengaluru, while promising a 25.40% monthly return. The informant and spouse transferred INR 53.5 lakh and received several initial payouts totalling INR 5.83 lakh before payments stopped. Attempts to locate the advertised offices failed. The bail record also describes investigation of an account linked to the petitioner, who denied knowledge and said money had been deposited by her husband. The case is useful for separating a highly reconstructable victim-facing corporate façade from comparatively weak public attribution to individual downstream participants.
cases.research_notes: Exact incident dates are left blank because the bail order supports the 2023 incident/FIR context but not a complete day-level attack interval. The petitioner-specific deposit amount is not used as the focal loss.

actors.function_assignment_basis: The source names several asserted company personnel/personas but does not independently resolve those labels to specific real-world humans.
actors.conduct_assessed: Operating the purported investment company through calls, WhatsApp, email, website, forged agreements and false office representations.
actors.attribution_limitations: Names may be personas or asserted company identities; the bail order does not establish human resolution for the victim-facing conduct.

actors.function_assignment_basis: Victim transfers and investigation of account-linked participants are documented, but the public bail order gives uneven actor-specific detail.
actors.conduct_assessed: Receiving/routing the victim's investment payments and making initial payout transfers.
actors.attribution_limitations: The source does not establish that each account-linked person knew or participated in the victim-facing scheme; petitioner-specific figures are themselves reported inconsistently.
actors.alternative_explanation: The petitioner said deposits to her account came from her husband and she knew nothing of the scheme.

cases.case_title: Port Blair digital-arrest fraud and co-accused-only mastermind allegation
cases.court_or_authority: Calcutta High Court, Circuit Bench at Port Blair
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Unknown digital-arrest caller(s)
cases.initial_contact_summary: A woman in Andaman and Nicobar Islands received calls from unknown persons and was subjected to a digital-arrest scheme.
cases.pretext_summary: The callers used a coercive digital-arrest scenario to compel transfers, but the bail order does not reproduce the full impersonated-agency script.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Coercive digital-arrest framing.
cases.requested_action: Transfer funds to accounts specified by the unknown callers.
cases.victim_action: The victim transferred INR 10,000,000 into three different accounts.
cases.other_evidence: One beneficiary-account holder was apprehended; the alleged mastermind theory was described as arising from that co-accused's statement.
cases.attribution_target: Muliyasiya Anil Sarman's alleged coordinating/mastermind role and the beneficiary-account network.
cases.attribution_limitations: The High Court expressly observed that, apart from the co-accused's statement, investigators had not unearthed other material apparently showing the petitioner's involvement. The original victim-facing caller(s) remained unresolved.
cases.alternative_explanation: The petitioner denied involvement, had cooperated before arrest and challenged the arrest process; the public order contains no independent digital linkage establishing a mastermind role.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Independent communications, device, telecom or financial evidence connecting the petitioner to the victim-facing callers or orchestration of the three beneficiary accounts.
cases.legal_provisions: Information Technology Act Section 66D; IPC Section 419; IPC Section 420; IPC Section 120B
cases.disposition: Calcutta High Court Circuit Bench at Port Blair granted bail on 5 February 2026, noting both arrest-procedure concerns and the absence of apparent independent material beyond a co-accused statement linking the petitioner.
cases.case_summary: A woman in Andaman and Nicobar Islands was subjected to a digital-arrest scheme by unknown callers and transferred INR 1 crore into three accounts. Investigators apprehended one beneficiary-account holder associated with INR 20 lakh; two other account holders were described as absconding. The prosecution said that the arrested account holder's statement identified Muliyasiya Anil Sarman as the mastermind. In the bail order, however, the High Court expressly noted that investigators had not unearthed other apparent material, apart from that co-accused statement, showing the petitioner's involvement. The case is therefore unusually valuable for the Atlas because it sharply separates a strong reconstruction of financial endpoints from weak public evidence for a claimed organiser and from the still-unresolved identity of the original digital-arrest caller.
cases.research_notes: Exact incident date is not inferred from FIR date. Attribution strength is intentionally limited despite the prosecution's 'mastermind' label.

actors.function_assignment_basis: The source states the victim was compelled by unknown phone callers to transfer funds but does not resolve their human identities.
actors.conduct_assessed: Conducting the phone-based digital-arrest coercion and directing transfers.
actors.attribution_limitations: The bail order provides no telecom/platform/device linkage identifying the caller(s).

actors.function_assignment_basis: Three receiving accounts are documented; one account holder was apprehended and two were described as absconding.
actors.conduct_assessed: Receiving the INR 1 crore loss through three accounts, including one account that received INR 20 lakh.
actors.attribution_limitations: The public order does not resolve all account holders or establish equivalent knowledge of the digital-arrest scheme.

actors.function_assignment_basis: The prosecution called him the mastermind based on an arrested co-accused's statement; the High Court found no other apparent material linking him after substantial investigation.
actors.conduct_assessed: Alleged orchestration/mastermind role in the digital-arrest racket.
actors.attribution_limitations: The High Court expressly noted the apparent absence of independent supporting material beyond the co-accused statement.
actors.alternative_explanation: He denied involvement and had cooperated with investigators before arrest.

cases.case_title: Terrorism-pretext police and ATS digital-arrest fraud
cases.impersonated_identity_detail: Delhi Police Inspector, Senior Inspector, ATS Pune officials and purported terrorism-case authorities
cases.reconnaissance_description: The callers elicited/ascertained the couple's assets, liabilities and retirement benefits before directing transfers.
cases.initial_contact_summary: An elderly complainant received a call from a woman claiming to be Inspector Anita Verma from Delhi Police Headquarters and saying the complainant's husband was involved in terrorist activity.
cases.pretext_summary: The call was escalated through purported senior police and ATS officials, with claims of a Jammu & Kashmir terrorism case, arrest warrants, secrecy instructions and hourly reporting requirements.
cases.other_psychological_mechanism: Multi-agency authority escalation, purported arrest warrants, surveillance-style reporting and asset interrogation.
cases.requested_action: Remain at home, keep the matter secret, report hourly, disclose assets/liabilities and transfer funds to specified accounts.
cases.victim_action: The complainant and husband complied under fear and transferred a total of INR 9,450,000.
cases.other_evidence: Ritu Gupta's account received INR 4,000,000 from the focal loss; prosecution alleged same-day onward transfers and deletion of WhatsApp content from her phone.
cases.attribution_target: Ritu Gupta's financial-endpoint role and the unresolved police/ATS impersonating caller cluster.
cases.attribution_limitations: The applicant was not identified as a victim-facing caller. She admitted the INR 4 million credit but claimed that co-accused had obtained and misused her bank details and SIM. The bail court considered that explanation implausible only prima facie.
cases.alternative_explanation: Ritu Gupta claimed she was herself cheated, had given bank details and SIM to proposed investors and later complained that they were being misused.
cases.primary_evidentiary_gap: Communications/device evidence showing whether the applicant knowingly coordinated with the digital-arrest callers, and recovery/authentication of deleted WhatsApp material.
cases.legal_provisions: BNS Section 308; BNS Section 318(4); BNS Section 319
cases.disposition: Delhi High Court dismissed Ritu Gupta's regular bail application on 16 March 2026; allegations remained to be tested at trial.
cases.case_summary: An elderly Delhi couple were told by callers posing as police and ATS officials that they were implicated in terrorism. The callers escalated the story across multiple asserted authorities, showed purported arrest warrants, ordered secrecy and hourly reporting, and obtained information about assets and retirement benefits. The couple transferred INR 94.5 lakh. The focal bail applicant's account received INR 40 lakh; the prosecution said she retained INR 33 lakh, moved the balance to 20 accounts and deleted WhatsApp content. She countered that co-accused had obtained and misused her bank details and SIM and that she had herself complained. The bail court rejected that explanation only on a prima facie basis. The case strongly illustrates the Atlas distinction between a well-resolved financial endpoint and an unresolved victim-facing deception layer.
cases.research_notes: This is the previously deferred CAND-0031, now admitted under Wave 1A. Screening history should be updated in place rather than creating a duplicate candidate.

actors.function_assignment_basis: The source reconstructs multiple purported police/ATS personas but does not identify the humans operating those calls.
actors.conduct_assessed: Delivering the terrorism accusation, arrest-warrant threats, secrecy/hourly-reporting instructions and transfer demands.
actors.attribution_limitations: The victim-facing humans remain unresolved in the reviewed bail order.

actors.function_assignment_basis: Her account received INR 40 lakh from the focal victim; prosecution alleged she retained INR 33 lakh, sent INR 7 lakh onward to 20 accounts and deleted WhatsApp content.
actors.conduct_assessed: Receiving and allegedly redistributing a major portion of the focal victim's transfer.
actors.attribution_limitations: She was not linked to the victim-facing calls and claimed her bank details/SIM had been misused by co-accused; the bail court rejected this only prima facie.
actors.alternative_explanation: She claimed to be a fraud victim who had handed over banking credentials/SIM for proposed investment and later complained of misuse.
